qualification: Cambridge International AS Level English Language 9093 (syllabus v2, examined 2024-2026)

items.prompt: What counts as evidence in an analysis of a text?
items.canonical_answer: Evidence means the exact words from the text that show the feature a point is about. A claim without it is only assertion: "the writer makes the flood feel alive" needs the words that do it, and the quotation is the proof. Evidence is not decoration after a point; it is what the point is about.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the exact words from the text that show the feature.
An answer about general supporting facts has taken a different sense of the term.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Select the exact words that carry a feature, and interpret them precisely in their context

items.prompt: State the steps for selecting evidence from a text.
items.canonical_answer: First, fix the feature the point is about — a verb, an image, a structural move. Then find the words that carry it. Then quote the shortest stretch that still shows it: three words that do the work beat three lines that surround them. Then check the quotation against the point: if the words quoted do not visibly carry the feature, the selection was wrong.
marking_guidance: Credit the steps in order: fix the feature, find the words, quote the shortest stretch, check the match.
The order exists so the words chosen serve the point, not the reverse.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Select the exact words that carry a feature, and interpret them precisely in their context

items.prompt: Here is an extract, written for the purpose: "The mayor swept into the hall, trailed by cameras, and announced that the repairs would begin ‘in due course’." Select the three words that best show the writer’s attitude, and interpret one of them.
items.canonical_answer: The three words: "swept", "trailed" and "‘in due course’". "Swept" gives the mayor a theatrical entrance rather than an arrival; "trailed" makes the cameras followers rather than witnesses; "‘in due course’" in inverted commas suggests a promise with no date in it. Interpreting the last: it means the repairs will happen sometime, and it suggests the writer doubts the sometime — the quotation marks let the reader hear the mayor’s own vagueness, so the reader waits with the writer for a date that never arrives in the sentence.
marking_guidance: Credit three words chosen from the extract, because the words are the evidence.
The interpretation must give both the meaning in place and what it suggests, so the words show the attitude.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Select the exact words that carry a feature, and interpret them precisely in their context

items.prompt: What is the difference between a quotation and a paraphrase as evidence, and why does only one of them count?
items.canonical_answer: A quotation is the text’s own words; a paraphrase is the writer’s retelling. Only a quotation counts as evidence because the feature lives in the exact words: "shrugged off its chains" shows the personification, and "describes the water breaking free" merely asserts it. The difference is that one can be checked against the page and the other can only be trusted, and analysis asks a reader to check.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: the text’s own words against a retelling.
Must say why: the feature lives in the exact words, so the check is only possible against the quotation.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Select the exact words that carry a feature, and interpret them precisely in their context

items.prompt: Read this sentence, written for the purpose: "The clinic has been ‘temporarily’ relocated to the sports hall." Interpret the word "temporarily": what does it mean here, and what does it suggest?
items.canonical_answer: The word means the move is not permanent, and the inverted commas suggest the writer doubts that: a detail that signals the writer’s own scepticism about the promise. The reader is led to expect the arrangement to last, and to read the rest of the piece looking for the evidence that it will — which the word "temporarily", quoted in this way, has already planted.
marking_guidance: Must give the meaning in place: the move is not permanent.
Must give what the detail suggests: the inverted commas implies the writer’s own doubt, so the reader should expect the move to last — what the word suggests beyond its meaning.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Select the exact words that carry a feature, and interpret them precisely in their context

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The writer uses language to make the reader sympathise with the farmers." What is missing, and what is the rule it breaks?
items.canonical_answer: The error is an analytical point with no words from the text to support it: the sentence names an effect and offers nothing that produces it, so a reader cannot check it and it carries no weight. The rule is that every point stands on quoted evidence — the two or three words that do the sympathising — and the fix is to add them: which words, from which sentence, doing what.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: an effect claimed with no quoted words under it.
Must give the fix: quote the words that produce the effect, instead of asserting it.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Select the exact words that carry a feature, and interpret them precisely in their context

items.prompt: What is an embedded quotation?
items.canonical_answer: An embedded quotation is a short quotation worked into the grammar of your own sentence, so the analysis and its evidence arrive together: "The verb ‘shrugged’ gives the river a body." The quotation is part of the sentence rather than a line dropped beside it, which is why the reader never leaves the argument to find the evidence.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: a short quotation inside the grammar of your own sentence.
The point of embedding — evidence and analysis arriving together — is part of the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Quote briefly and aptly, so that every word quoted is a word analysed

items.prompt: Give the steps for embedding a quotation.
items.canonical_answer: First choose a short phrase, the two or three words that carry the feature. Then fit it into your sentence’s grammar so it reads as part of your sentence — the quotation becomes the subject or the object of your own verb. Then comment on the words inside it, beginning the analysis immediately, because the embedding exists so the comment can start at once.
marking_guidance: Credit the steps in order: choose, fit into the grammar, comment at once.
An answer that stops at "put it in quotation marks" has missed the grammar and the comment.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Quote briefly and aptly, so that every word quoted is a word analysed

items.prompt: Embed the phrase "a town holding its breath" in an analytical sentence of your own, and comment on it.
items.canonical_answer: The town "holding its breath" is personified as a crowd waiting for a result, so the reader is positioned inside the anticipation rather than outside it. (Any sentence that works the phrase into its own grammar and then comments on the words inside it meets the task: the embedding is the fit, the analysis is the comment.)
marking_guidance: Credit the embedding: the phrase fitted into the sentence’s grammar, because the fit is the skill.
Credit the comment on the words inside the phrase, so the analysis follows the evidence.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Quote briefly and aptly, so that every word quoted is a word analysed

items.prompt: Why is a two-word quotation often stronger than a quoted sentence?
items.canonical_answer: The reason is that every word quoted can then be analysed: a two-word quotation leaves nowhere to hide, and the analysis either engages with those words or visibly fails to. A quoted sentence is mostly padding, and only two or three of its words were ever doing the work, so the rest blurs the feature the analysis is pointing at.
marking_guidance: Credit the reason: each quoted word can be analysed, so short keeps the analysis honest.
An answer about saving words has missed the analytical reason.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Quote briefly and aptly, so that every word quoted is a word analysed

items.prompt: What is the difference between a line reference and a quotation, and what does the line reference fail to do?
items.canonical_answer: A line reference is a location ("in line 14") and a quotation is the words themselves. The line reference fails to show the choice: it tells a reader where to look but leaves the finding to them, substituting a map reference for the thing itself. A quotation puts the evidence in front of the reader, which is what analysis owes its reader.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: a location against the words themselves.
Must say what the reference fails to do: show the choice, leaving the reader to hunt for it.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Quote briefly and aptly, so that every word quoted is a word analysed

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The writer creates sympathy in lines 8–12." What is wrong with this as evidence, and what should replace it?
items.canonical_answer: The error is citing a range of lines instead of the words that matter: the reader is sent hunting for the feature instead of being shown it, and five lines of text are treated as evidence when only two or three words inside them were doing the work. The replacement quotes those words — "the ‘cracked’ bowl she still kept" — and analyses them, so the evidence is in front of the reader and the analysis begins at once.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: a range of lines where the words were needed.
Must give the replacement: the two or three words, quoted and analysed.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Quote briefly and aptly, so that every word quoted is a word analysed

items.prompt: Name five analytical verbs that link evidence to effect, and say what each is for.
items.canonical_answer: Suggests (leaves room, suits an implication); conveys (names what is carried by the words); evokes (names a feeling summoned in the reader); positions (says what the writer does to the reader’s stance); undercuts (says a later choice undoes an earlier one). Each verb states a different mechanism, which is why choosing among them is itself an act of analysis.
marking_guidance: Credit at least five verbs of this feature-set with what each is for: suggests, conveys, evokes, positions, undercuts.
The verbs must be analytical ones that join evidence to effect, not narrative ones that retell.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Join evidence to comment with precise analytical language, not stock phrases

items.prompt: What separates a precise statement of effect from a stock one, and what is the test?
items.canonical_answer: A stock phrase could follow any quotation anywhere — "this engages the reader" — because it was written for every text and so for none. A precise statement could have been written for these words only: it names what this reader is led to think, feel or do, and it fits the quoted words and them alone. The test is the swap: put the phrase after a quotation from a different text, and if it still works, it is stock.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: written for any quotation against written for these words only.
Must give the test: the swap to another quotation, which a precise statement survives and a stock one does not.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Join evidence to comment with precise analytical language, not stock phrases

items.prompt: Rewrite this stock comment as a precise one: "The word ‘huddle’ creates a picture and engages the reader."
items.canonical_answer: A precise version: "The verb ‘huddle’ makes the shacks press together for warmth, so the reader sees the settlement as a living thing trying to keep itself warm, and the blame lands on whoever left it cold." The stock version could follow any word; the rewrite names what "huddle" suggests — bodies, warmth, closeness — and what it makes this reader do, which is pity and blame.
marking_guidance: Credit the rewrite: the specific association named, because the words are the evidence.
The rewrite must say what the reader is led to think or feel, so the effect is theirs and not a generic "engaged reader".
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Join evidence to comment with precise analytical language, not stock phrases

items.prompt: Rewrite this comment so that it names the audience affected: "The list of three makes the reader want to visit."
items.canonical_answer: A rewritten version: "The list of three — beach, bakery, harbour — gives the browsing tourist a manageable day, so the reader deciding where to go is handed three things to picture, and the deciding is done for them." The generic "reader" is replaced by the text’s own audience, the person planning a trip, and the effect is named as theirs: a decision made easy.
marking_guidance: Credit the rewrite: the text’s own audience named, because the effect belongs to them.
The effect must be what that audience is led to do, so the sentence shows the mechanism on the named reader.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Join evidence to comment with precise analytical language, not stock phrases

items.prompt: A learner ends every analytical sentence with "which engages the reader". What is the problem, and how can the learner spot it?
items.canonical_answer: The problem is a stock effect phrase that could follow any quotation: it analyses nothing, because the words quoted and the effect named never meet. The learner can spot it with the swap test — move the phrase to a sentence about a different text, and if it still fits, it is stock — and fix it by naming what these particular words make this particular reader think, feel or do, so the effect could belong to no other quotation.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: a phrase that could follow any quotation.
Must give the test: the swap to another quotation, and the fix of a matched, specific effect.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Join evidence to comment with precise analytical language, not stock phrases

items.prompt: What four parts does an analytical paragraph contain?
items.canonical_answer: A claim about the text, the evidence that shows it, the analysis of what the evidence does, and the link to the text’s purpose. The four are a unit: a claim without evidence is assertion, evidence without analysis is quotation, and analysis without the link to purpose stops one sentence short of the mark.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning of all four parts: claim, evidence, analysis, link to purpose.
The parts are named as a unit, so an answer with three of them has defined a shorter shape.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Build analytical paragraphs into one coherent argument about the text

items.prompt: Give the four moves for building an analytical paragraph, in order.
items.canonical_answer: First state the claim: what the text is doing here. Then quote the few words that show it, embedded in your sentence. Then analyse what those words do to this reader. Then link that effect to the text’s purpose: how it serves what the text is for. Four moves, in that order, until they are habit.
marking_guidance: Credit the four steps in order: claim, evidence, analysis, link.
The order matters because each move feeds the next, so a paragraph that starts with evidence has begun in the middle.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Build analytical paragraphs into one coherent argument about the text

items.prompt: What does a coherent line of argument across a whole analysis contain?
items.canonical_answer: It contains a single view of the text, stated at the opening; paragraphs that each advance the view from a different side; and links between them that carry the reader from one to the next. The reader leaves convinced of something rather than informed of many things, which is the difference between an argument and a pile.
marking_guidance: Credit the features: one view stated, paragraphs advancing it, links carrying the reader.
An answer about writing more paragraphs has counted them instead of joining them.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Build analytical paragraphs into one coherent argument about the text

items.prompt: What is the difference between an argument about a text and a list of observations on it?
items.canonical_answer: An argument organises its observations as evidence for a view: each one is there to prove something, and its place in the whole is decided by what it proves. A list sets observations side by side and lets them add up, or not, by accident: a metaphor, a short sentence and a direct address sit together with nothing making them mean one thing. The difference is whether a reader leaves convinced or merely informed.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: observations as evidence for a view against observations side by side.
Must say what the difference does: the reader is convinced by an argument and only informed by a list.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Build analytical paragraphs into one coherent argument about the text

items.prompt: Two paragraphs on the same extract. A: "The writer uses a metaphor and a short sentence. The metaphor is effective and the short sentence adds impact." B: "The writer’s metaphor — ‘the town licked its wounds’ — makes the community a single hurt body, and the short sentence that follows, ‘Nobody counted.’, lands as a verdict after the long accounting of losses. Both choices serve the piece’s purpose: they turn statistics into a body that a reader can pity." Which makes the stronger point, and what is the case against the weaker one?
items.canonical_answer: B makes the stronger point: it quotes the words, analyses what they do to this reader (a single hurt body; a verdict after accounting), and links both to the purpose of turning figures into pity. The case against A is that it names two features and attaches stock praise — "effective", "adds impact" — that could follow any quotation, so no evidence is shown and no effect is stated. A could be written about any text with a metaphor and a short sentence; B could only be written about this one, which is the judgement.
marking_guidance: Credit the judgement: B, with reasons drawn from its evidence and matched effects; however, note what A does have — two true observations — because the weak version is not worthless, only unsupported.
Credit the case against A: stock praise with no quoted words, which no reader can check.
The strongest answers note the test: B could not survive being moved to another text, which A could.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Build analytical paragraphs into one coherent argument about the text

items.prompt: An analysis reads: "The writer uses a metaphor. The writer uses short sentences. The writer uses direct address. The writer uses a statistic." What is wrong, and what would join these into an analysis?
items.canonical_answer: The error is a string of separate observations with nothing joining them into a view of the text: four true sentences that together say nothing, because no claim organises them. The fix is the argument: decide what the text is doing to its reader — pressing a worried resident to act, say — and make each observation a witness: the metaphor carries the threat, the short sentences land the urgency, the direct address names who must act, the statistic makes the threat measurable. The observations were the raw material; the view of the text is the analysis.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: observations with no claim joining them.
Must give the fix: one view of the text, with each observation turned into evidence for it.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Build analytical paragraphs into one coherent argument about the text

items.prompt:
Read this extract, written for the purpose:

Nobody plans to end up at the Oshakati night market at nine on a Tuesday, but the market plans for you. The gates are lit like a harbour, the smoke from the braai stands drifts across the road, and the noise arrives before you do: three languages, two radios, one argument about football that never quite finishes. The vendors know their trade. "You will not find a better avocado in the north," says a woman who has clearly said so to every passer-by since the sun went down. She is not wrong, either. By ten the crowd thickens, the benches fill, and the whole place settles into the business of feeding strangers until they are no longer strange.

Write one analytical paragraph of about 120 words, containing at least three short embedded quotations, about how the extract works on its reader.
items.canonical_answer: The feature draws its reader in through the senses before it makes any argument. The market "plans for you" personifies the place as a host, so the reader arrives as an invited guest rather than a customer, and the "smoke… drifts across the road" gives the scene a smell before it has a price. The noise "arrives before you do", a fronted clause that puts the reader in motion towards it, and the trilingual clamour makes the market a place where many communities meet rather than a single street. The vendor’s quoted boast, "You will not find a better avocado in the north", is theatre the writer clearly enjoys: the superlative and the word "clearly" let the reader hear both the sales pitch and the writer’s wry affection for it. The final sentence completes the design — "feeding strangers until they are no longer strange" — because the paragraph’s sensory welcome has been arguing all along that the market turns a crowd into a community, which is what a reader deciding to go is really being sold.
marking_guidance: Credit the paragraph’s evidence: at least three short quotations, embedded in the sentences, because the words are the proof.
Credit the effect named for each quotation, and the audience it is named for, so the analysis runs feature to evidence to effect.
Credit the paragraph’s shape: a claim, then evidence, then analysis, then a link to the extract’s purpose, which is the structure to reward.
Do not credit retelling of what the extract says: the words quoted are the evidence, and what they do to the reader is the analysis.

items.prompt:
Read this extract, written for the purpose:

My grandmother’s kitchen had one rule and it was never spoken: watch first, ask later. So for three years I watched her make the Sunday bread — the flour poured in a spiral, the salt measured in her palm because a spoon, she said, was for people who did not know their hands — and I asked nothing. I learned the loaf by its sounds. The dough is ready when it stops being loud. The oven is right when the first breath through the door smells like Sunday. And when she finally handed me the bowl, she said only: "You have been baking since you were eleven. You were just standing at the wrong end of the table."

Write one analytical paragraph of about 120 words, containing at least three short embedded quotations, about how the extract works on its reader.
items.canonical_answer: The memoir teaches through the grandmother’s voice without ever stating a lesson. The rule "watch first, ask later" is set out in a minor sentence at the opening, so its brevity performs the discipline it describes, and the long sentence that follows — with its dashes holding the flour "poured in a spiral" and the salt "measured in her palm" — makes the reader watch slowly too, clause by clause, as the writer once did. The imperative-like fragments "The dough is ready when it stops being loud" carry the kitchen’s sound wisdom in the grandmother’s cadence, so the reader is taught the loaf by ear, exactly as the writer was. The closing quotation — "You were just standing at the wrong end of the table" — reframes three years of watching as apprenticeship rather than exclusion, and the reader, who has also spent the paragraph watching, discovers they have been learning the same lesson, which is how the extract makes its quiet point about knowledge passed by presence.
marking_guidance: Credit the paragraph’s evidence: at least three short quotations, embedded in the sentences, because the words are the proof.
Credit the effect named for each quotation, and the audience it is named for, so the analysis runs feature to evidence to effect.
Credit the paragraph’s shape: a claim, then evidence, then analysis, then a link to the extract’s purpose, which is the structure to reward.
Do not credit retelling of what the extract says: the words quoted are the evidence, and what they do to the reader is the analysis.

items.prompt:
Read this extract, written for the purpose:

Your child can read this sentence. Half the children in this district cannot. That single fact should keep every parent awake tonight. The reading gap in our schools is not a statistic; it is a queue of small chairs outside a room that never opens. We are asking you to fund one hour of reading help, twice a week, for three hundred children who have already been left waiting. One hour. Twice a week. The cost is one textbook per family. The result, in two years, is a district where "cannot" starts to shrink. Give the hour. The children have already given the wait.

Write one analytical paragraph of about 120 words, containing at least three short embedded quotations, about how the extract works on its reader.
items.canonical_answer: The leaflet opens with a trap built on the reader’s own literacy: "Your child can read this sentence" flatters and implicates at once, because the reader has just proved the claim by reading, and "Half the children in this district cannot" turns that proof into guilt. The statistic is then refused as a statistic — "not a statistic; it is a queue of small chairs" — and the metaphor converts an abstract gap into an image a worried parent can see, which is the leaflet’s central move: numbers become children. The repetition "One hour. Twice a week." lands as a manageable request after the unmanageable image, so the reader is offered relief precisely when the pressure peaked. The final pair of short sentences, "Give the hour. The children have already given the wait.", balances what the reader must do against what the children have endured, and the leave-taking is a debt the reader can discharge for the price the leaflet named.
marking_guidance: Credit the paragraph’s evidence: at least three short quotations, embedded in the sentences, because the words are the proof.
Credit the effect named for each quotation, and the audience it is named for, so the analysis runs feature to evidence to effect.
Credit the paragraph’s shape: a claim, then evidence, then analysis, then a link to the extract’s purpose, which is the structure to reward.
Do not credit retelling of what the extract says: the words quoted are the evidence, and what they do to the reader is the analysis.

items.prompt:
Read this extract, written for the purpose:

The Ondjiva Music Festival promised three stages and delivered one that worked, and this review will try to be fair about the difference. The good first: the headline act arrived, the sound on the main stage was crisp and warm, and the crowd — rain-soaked and unbothered — sang the choruses back at a band that clearly had not expected to be loved that hard. The bad: the second stage never opened its doors, the food stalls ran out of everything except disappointment by six, and the site map was a rumour. The headline act played ninety minutes and forgave the organisers everything. The audience was less forgiving about the queues, and on the evidence of the exits, next year’s tickets will not sell themselves.

Write one analytical paragraph of about 120 words, containing at least three short embedded quotations, about how the extract works on its reader.
items.canonical_answer: The review earns its verdicts by showing its working. The opening states the facts as a promise kept only in part — "promised three stages and delivered one that worked" — and the structure announces the method: fairness "about the difference", good before bad, evidence for both. The rain-soaked crowd "unbothered" and singing "back at a band that clearly had not expected to be loved that hard" gives the one triumph a cause the reader can hear, while the failures come in an escalating tricolon — a stage unopened, stalls emptied, the site map "a rumour", a metaphor that turns the organiser’s own tool into a fiction. The final judgement is left to arithmetic rather than adjectives: the band "forgave the organisers everything", the audience "was less forgiving about the queues", and tickets "will not sell themselves", so the reader performs the subtraction the review has staged. The review’s verdict lives in that closing balance, and the extract has taught the reader to check it, which is what a review owes its reader.
marking_guidance: Credit the paragraph’s evidence: at least three short quotations, embedded in the sentences, because the words are the proof.
Credit the effect named for each quotation, and the audience it is named for, so the analysis runs feature to evidence to effect.
Credit the paragraph’s shape: a claim, then evidence, then analysis, then a link to the extract’s purpose, which is the structure to reward.
Do not credit retelling of what the extract says: the words quoted are the evidence, and what they do to the reader is the analysis.
